problem: “swept away” for “broken in upon” shifts the sense (being disturbed or interrupted, not carried off).
replacement: People who live in democratic countries do not care for the simple, rowdy, or coarse amusements that the common people enjoy in aristocratic communities; they find such pastimes childish or dull. Nor are they any more drawn to the intellectual and refined entertainments of the aristocratic classes. They want something productive and substantial in their pleasures; they want to mix real gain with their enjoyment. In aristocratic communities the people readily surrender to outbursts of noisy, boisterous merriment, which at once drives away the memory of their hardships. The natives of democracies do not like being disturbed so violently, and they never lose sight of themselves without regret. In place of these frivolous delights they prefer quieter, more serious amusements, which resemble business and do not push business entirely out of their minds. An American, instead of going out in a spare hour to dance merrily at some public gathering place, as other men of his occupation still do over most of Europe, shuts himself up at home to drink. He thus enjoys two pleasures: he can keep thinking about his business, and he can get drunk respectably beside his own fireside.

problem: “violence” sharpens “vehemence”; “settled” does not carry “constituted” (having established institutions).
replacement: In an orderly and established democracy like the United States, where men cannot get rich by war, by public office, or by political confiscation, the love of wealth drives them chiefly into business and manufacturing. Although these pursuits often cause great upheavals and disasters, they cannot prosper without strictly regular habits and a long routine of small, uniform acts. The stronger the passion, the more regular these habits and the more uniform these acts. It may be said that the vehemence of their desires is what makes the Americans so methodical; it disturbs their minds, but it disciplines their lives.

problem: “Picture travelers…” turns his simile into an instruction to the reader and splits the comparison; the source says “Like travellers…”.
replacement: The remark I apply here to America could in fact be made of almost all our contemporaries. Variety is disappearing from the human race; the same ways of acting, thinking, and feeling are found all over the world. This is not only because nations have more influence on one another and imitate one another more faithfully. It is also because the men of each country give up more and more the distinctive opinions and feelings of a caste, a profession, or a family, and so arrive together at something nearer to the nature of man, which is the same everywhere. Thus they grow more alike, even without having imitated one another. Like travelers scattered through a large forest crossed by paths that all converge on one point, if every one of them keeps his eyes fixed on that point and moves toward it, they draw imperceptibly closer together, though they do not seek one another, do not see one another, and do not know one another; and they will be surprised in the end to find themselves all gathered on the same spot. All the nations that take as the object of their studies and their imitation not any particular man but man himself are tending in the end toward a similar state of society, like these travelers converging on the central clearing of the forest.
